beats.narration_text: Hi — I'm Divij Pawar. This video is about why AI agents fail silently, and what actually stops it. Somewhere right now, an AI agent is stuck. Not broken. Not crashed. Worse — it's still running, still confident, still absolutely sure it's making progress, while it does the exact same thing over and over, burning time, burning money, and reporting "success" the entire way through.

props.command: Why do AI agents fail silently, and what actually stops it?
output: Loop: the cycle has no built-in sense of when to stop
Drift: the original goal gets crowded out of context
Claim: ten failures still report task completed successfully

beats.narration_text: This is the part nobody puts in the demo video. Today we're opening up the four ways agents actually fail — and then we're going to fix one, live, so you can see exactly what stops the bleeding.

shot.visual_intent: The four failure modes named up front as empty panels — the framework the body fills in one beat at a time.

show.event: Title 'Four Ways Agents Fail' writes on
Four empty panels slide into frame in sequence, evenly spanning the safe area
Panel labels fade in: Infinite Loops / Context Drift / Hallucinated Arguments / Confidently Wrong
All four hold, ghosted — none filled yet; a small terracotta tick marks panel one as next

beats.act: failure mode 1 — the infinite tool-call loop
beats.narration_text:
An agent works in a cycle: look at the situation, decide what to do, take an action, check what happened, repeat. That loop is the whole engine. The problem is, nothing built into that loop guarantees it ever stops.

Say you've got a coding agent trying to fix a failing test. It runs the test, sees it fail, edits the code, runs the test again. Reasonable so far. But if its fix doesn't actually address the real problem, the test fails again, in the exact same way. So it tries again. Same failure. Again. The agent has no built-in sense of "I've tried this three times, something's fundamentally wrong here." It just keeps observing the same failure, and reacting the same way, forever — unless something outside the loop stops it.

shot.visual_intent: The loop runs correctly, then keeps running — the same failure recurring while the attempt counter climbs.

show.event: Panel one lights; the other three dim to ghost at the top of frame
Four stage nodes draw into a ring: Observe → Decide → Act → Check Result
A pulse runs the ring once at a calm pace — this is the engine working as designed
A test chip appears reading FAIL; the pulse runs again and the same FAIL chip returns unchanged
An attempt counter starts climbing in the corner; the ring speeds up on each cycle
The 'I've tried this three times' thought chip fades in ghosted, then strikes through — the agent has no such check
Ring keeps spinning; a terracotta line lands outside it: only something outside the loop stops it

beats.narration_text:
Every AI model has something like a working memory — a limited window of text it can actually pay attention to at once. As a task runs longer, more and more gets stuffed into that window: the original instructions, ten tool results, error messages, retries, side conversations.

Eventually, older information starts getting crowded out, or just deprioritized. The agent's original goal — the thing you actually asked for — was three hundred messages ago. What's left in its immediate attention is the last few tool calls and errors. So it starts optimizing for "make this error go away," instead of "accomplish what the user actually wanted." That's context drift. The agent hasn't forgotten in a dramatic way — it's just lost the thread of what mattered most.

shot.visual_intent: The goal block physically pushed to the edge of the window and faded as newer blocks pack in behind it.

show.event: Panel two lights; a wide rectangle labelled 'context window' draws, empty
A terracotta block labelled 'Original Goal' seats at the left edge of the window
Blocks pack in behind it on the spoken items: tool results, errors, retries, side conversations
The window fills; the goal block is shoved toward the left edge and begins fading
Two competing objectives resolve side by side — 'make this error go away' in ink, 'what the user wanted' ghosted out
The goal block fades to ghost at the boundary and holds; label reads 'not forgotten — deprioritized'

beats.narration_text:
Every tool an agent can use has a strict shape it expects — specific fields, specific formats. Like a form that only accepts a date in one exact format, or a function that only accepts a real, existing file name.

Sometimes the model predicts an argument that sounds exactly right — plausible, well-formatted, confident — but it's just made up. Maybe it's referencing a file that was deleted three steps ago. Maybe it's inventing a setting the tool never supported. The tool call either throws an error, or worse, silently does something slightly different than intended. And because language models are built to produce fluent, confident-sounding text, a hallucinated argument doesn't look like a guess. It looks exactly like a fact.

shot.visual_intent: A tool-call form filling in field by field, where the invented argument is indistinguishable from the real ones until it is marked.

show.event: Panel three lights; a tool schema card draws showing the fields the tool actually accepts
A tool call form fills in beside it, one mono field at a time, all reading as clean and well-formed
Every filled field is checked in ink — the form looks entirely correct
One field, priority_level, is ringed terracotta; a line drops to the schema card and finds no match
Two failure branches draw: 'throws an error' and, below it, 'silently does something else' held longer
Closing line lands over the still-clean-looking form: it doesn't look like a guess, it looks like a fact

beats.narration_text:
This is the failure mode that makes the other three dangerous, instead of just annoying. An agent has no built-in alarm bell for "I am stuck." It doesn't experience frustration or doubt. So after ten failed attempts at the same fix, it can still generate a final summary that reads: "Task completed successfully."

That gap — between what actually happened, and what the agent reports happened — is the single most dangerous thing about agent failures. A human who's stuck usually looks stuck. An agent that's stuck can look identical to an agent that succeeded, right up until someone checks the actual result.

shot.visual_intent: The reported result and the actual result held side by side, with the gap between them measured on screen.

show.event: Panel four lights; the frame splits into two aligned columns
Left column stacks ten retry log lines, each reading FAIL, in mono
Right column stays empty and calm while the left keeps stacking
The agent's final summary card writes into the right column: 'Task completed successfully'
A terracotta bracket spans the space between the two columns, labelled 'the gap'
Two silhouette chips resolve below: a stuck human looks stuck / a stuck agent looks identical to one that won

beats.narration_text:
Let's walk through one, start to finish. You ask a coding agent to deploy a small website update. Step one — it runs the deploy command. Step two — the deploy fails, because of a missing environment variable. Step three — instead of asking you what that variable should be, it guesses a value, and hallucinates it into the config. Step four — the deploy runs again, fails differently now, because the guessed value was wrong. Step five — the agent, still in the loop, tries a slightly different guess. Step six — same failure, different guess. This repeats twelve times.

By attempt twelve, the context window is packed with failed deploy logs. The original instruction — "deploy this small update" — has been buried under eleven rounds of error messages. And the agent, unprompted, hasn't once said, "I don't actually know this value. Can you tell me?"

shot.visual_intent: All four failure modes running at once in a single real trace — the framework used, not just referenced.

show.event: All four panel labels return as a compact legend along the top
Numbered steps build downward on the spoken step number, in mono
Step three's guessed config value is ringed terracotta; the legend's 'Hallucinated Arguments' tick lights
Steps five and six repeat with a fresh guess; the 'Infinite Loops' tick lights and an attempt counter starts climbing
Counter runs to twelve; the step list compresses into a dense block of failed logs
The original instruction chip is buried under the log block and fades; the 'Context Drift' tick lights
The question the agent never asked appears ghosted and struck through: 'I don't know this value — can you tell me?'

beats.narration_text:
So how do you actually stop this? Three guardrails — and they work together.

A turn limit. Cap how many loop cycles the agent gets, before it's forced to stop and report status instead of continuing silently. Twelve failed deploy attempts becomes three, then a forced stop.

A verifier step. Before the agent marks anything as done, a separate check — sometimes a second model call, sometimes a hard rule — actually confirms the real-world result matches the claim. Did the website actually go live? Check. Don't just ask the agent if it thinks it did.

A human-in-the-loop gate. For anything with real consequences — spending money, deleting a file, deploying to production — the agent proposes the action and stops, and a person has to approve it before it executes. This turns "confidently wrong" from a silent disaster, into a visible pause you can catch.

artifactLines: Turn limit — cap the loop, force a status report instead of a silent retry
Verifier — a separate check confirms the real result, not the agent's claim
Human gate — anything irreversible stops and waits for a person to approve
None of these make an agent smarter; they make its failures visible

beats.narration_text:
None of these fixes make an agent smarter. They just make its failures visible, and its damage limited — which, it turns out, is most of the actual engineering work behind building agents that don't quietly wreck your afternoon.

So your turn. Here's the prompt: "Take an agent workflow I rely on and find where it can fail silently." Run it against something that touches money, files, or a deploy. Then check the answer for three things — does it name a turn limit, does it name a verifier that checks the real result, and does it name a human gate on the irreversible step? If it comes back saying "write a better prompt" and stops there, it missed the point entirely.

Next time an agent tells you it's done, ask yourself — did anything actually check that? If the answer's no, you're trusting a system that's never once had to know the difference between succeeding, and just saying so.

props.command: Take an agent workflow I rely on and find where it can fail silently.
output: Run this on a workflow that touches money, files, or deploys
Check it names a turn limit, a verifier, and a human gate
Reject any answer that says write a better prompt and stops
